passages.text:
In the natural world a multitude of symbiotic relationships has developed between different organisms. In many of these relationships, the partnership is one-sided; in other words, one of the symbionts benefits from the association while the other may be harmed by it.

Sometimes two species develop a relationship that is beneficial to both parties. This is called mutualism. A well-known example of such an alliance is found in the relationship of ants and aphids. Aphids are tiny pear-shaped insects that typically feed exclusively on a particular plant, living in crowded clusters on the underside of leaves or on stems. Their mouthparts are adapted to piercing plant tissue and efficiently sucking out the sap, not all of which they can metabolize. From the back of the insects two cornicles, or "tailpipes," protrude and from these, aphids secrete honeydew, a sticky substance high in nutritive value. The honeydew, which falls onto the ground or onto the leaves of the plant, is intercepted by ants, which use the substance as a food source.

Some ant species even stroke the back end of aphids - sometimes called "ants' cows" - with their legs and antennae in order to stimulate the flow of the liquid. Aphids may actually withhold the honeydew until ants caress them. Some ants take care of whole "herds" of aphids, building shelters for them and carrying them to new plants as the old ones die.

The ants, whose mouthparts are not well modified for obtaining juice from plants, rely on the aphids to obtain it for them. The aphids are not well adapted for fighting off predators and rely on ants to provide this service for them. Both these creatures, therefore, benefit from this arrangement of close cooperation in a relationship somewhat analogous to the relationship between cattle and human beings.

The erection of the Brooklyn Bridge, which spans the East River in New York City, vies with the digging of the Suez Canal as one of the great engineering triumphs of the nineteenth century. Approval for the project was given in 1866, but a setback occurred before work had gotten under way - John Roebling, its celebrated designer and chief engineer, died from tetanus. His son, Washington Roebling, took over the mammoth task and set to work supervising the placement of the foundations on the riverbed.

Because work had to be performed below water level, enormous watertight chambers called caissons were used. The bottom of the caissons was open and rested on the riverbed.  Well-like tubes extending above the water level allowed compressed air to be pumped in to prevent water from entering and to provide air for the workers excavating the soil on the open bottom.  The extracted debris was passed out of other vertical shafts. As the soil was removed, the caissons gradually sank into the riverbed until they rested securely on underlying rock. On their upper sides the two granite towers from which the bridge was suspended were built up to an eventual height of 270 feet above water level.

To support the weight of the 1,600-foot span of roadway, four immense spun-wire cables - each 16 inches in diameter - were ingeniously fed out from cast-iron blocks mounted on the tops of the completed towers. From the cables steel rope suspenders reached down to the roadway itself, and extra support was gained from steel stays leading directly from the towers to the deck.

During construction many novel problems were faced. One such predicament was caused by the compressed air pumped into the caissons. Workers ascending too rapidly through the decompression chambers suffered from the bends due to the formation of nitrogen bubbles in the blood. In 1872 Roebling himself became a victim of this crippling disease and spent the remainder of the building period supervising from his apartment overlooking the river. Roebling's wife, Emily, took over the practical day-to-day matters and became an expert herself on bridge construction.

Despite numerous accidents and engineering difficulties, and even some financial scandals, in 1883 the bridge, dubbed "a new wonder of the world," was finally opened to public traffic - a testament to the determination, skill, and daring of those who envisioned and built it.

A few investigators are dedicated to researching mysterious unclassified beasts that orthodox scientists refuse to believe exist. While these cryptozoologists keep an open mind about their object of study, they are quick to point to cases in which the skeptics have been proved mistaken. For example, the pygmy hippopotamus, once claimed to be extinct, was found to exist in East Africa. The giant squid was dismissed as the product of an overactive imagination until a specimen was washed up on a beach in 1873.

One of the most celebrated mysteries being investigated by cryptozoologists is Bigfoot - a large, hairy, humanoid creature that many people claim to have seen in parts of North America. In 1967, a film of what was purported to be Bigfoot was actually taken by an amateur photographer. Of course, this footage may well have been a hoax. Nevertheless, many people remain convinced of Bigfoot's existence.

The Loch Ness Monster provokes similar disagreements among researchers. |In this case some authorities argue that while some creature may have been seen, it is probably a type of whale that penetrates the loch when the Ness River floods.

The yeti, or abominable snowman, of the Himalayas may be the most fascinating undiscovered creature. Many climbers claim to have seen the yeti or its footprints, and local inhabitants of the mountains are convinced of its existence. As in the case of Bigfoot, some film footage that is alleged to be of this creature exists. No doubt, such well-known mysteries as the yeti and less well-known mysteries as the Congo dinosaur and the Queensland tiger are intriguing and will no doubt be the object of much speculation as well as pursuit for years to come.

lectureGroups.transcript:
In areas of land underlain by limestone and subject to water erosion, a distinctive type of landscape is formed. Rainwater, containing chemicals taken from the air and the soil, forms a%r	Á&z'T5L34-38Weak acid solution. This solution then seeps into cracks in the limestone and dissolves it, forming caves and channels.
Beneath the surface, the land may become honeycombed with caverns and underground streams. This process can take thousands of years. Here's a cross-sectional diagram of this kind of landscape.
A particular feature of this limestone landscape is called a sinkhole. Sinkholes are depressions in the ground, usually circular or oval in shape and varying in diameter from a few meters to a kilometer, and in depth from a few meters to several hundred.
Sometimes sinkholes are formed when an underground cavern collapses. This can be due to the weight of water soaking into the land above the underground cavity or because the cavern becomes too large to support the roof. These sinkholes usually have steep walls due to a sudden collapse of land. Sometimes a house or a section of a road can fall into a sinkhole when the ground collapses. The collapse-type sinkhole has beco more common in recent years due mainly to human activity, which often interferes with the natural flow of underground water.
Another kind of sinkhole is formed when water permeates the surface through cracks in the surface rock. As water continues to flow through these cracks, the hole gets larger, allowing more water to flow in. The sinkhole typically takes on a conical shape, with the roughly circular opening narrowing to a point at the place where the water disappears under the surface. If the bottom of the sinkhole reaches the water table, a lake may form.
In the past, these geological features were often thoughtlessly used as places to dump trash. This led directly to the pollution of groundwater, since sinkholes connect to the underground water system. Attempts are being made to improve this situation through educational programs, and today newly found sinkholes are often filled with soil or cement in an attempt to stop people from dumping their garbage in them.

lectureGroups.transcript:
Today we are going to be talking about one of the most basic laws of economics: nothing of value is free. Sometimes this is dubbed "tanstaafl." The word "tanstaafl" is formed from the initials of the statement "There Ain't No Such Thing As A Free Lunch." What this means is that everything that has value must be paid for in currency, labor, or something else.
Not only do people have to pay for everything that has value, but governments also have to. Governments have a lot ofown us that when taxes get too high, people eventually revolt and overthrow the offending government. To avoid raising taxes, a government must find another way to deal with the problem of getting money to meet its expenses.
Let's look at the Romans. The Roman government taxed its citizens in order to pay for the expenses of running such a vast empire. It became apparent over time that if it raised taxes further, it risked provoking unrest. So the leaders came up with the idea of clipping the denarius, a coin made of 94 percent silver. When the tax collectors brought in people's taxes paid in silver coins, the Roman treasury clipped, or shaved, the edges off the coins. The clippings were minted into new coins. For a time, this gave the government the money necessary for its budget. But it did not take the Roman people long to realize that some of their coins were missing silver. Therefore, they either refused to accept the clipped coins or charged more coins for their goods and svices. In later centuries a system called "reeding" came into practice. A reeded coin has grooves along its edge, making it easy to see whether or not clipping has taken place.
But since the Roman government still needed money and clipping no longer served its purpose, the Roman treasury started melting down coins and reminting them with a mixture of base metal, such as copper. However, each time a coin was melted down and reminted with a base-metal mixture, the percentage of precious metal became less and that of base metal more. When the Roman people realized that their money was being debased, they responded by hoarding coins. Whenever they got a "good" coin - one with a high percentage of silver in it - they kept it. They spent only "bad" coins - those with a low percentage of silver. This behavior is explained by Gresham's Law, which states that bad money drives good money out of circulation. When debasement happens, money loses its value and prices inevitably rise.
